tone_statements.citation: Alio, Khalil. 2009. Remarques comparatives sur le consonantisme entre le bidiya et le dangaléat. Lingua Posnaniensis 51: 7-18.
tone_statements.quote: Le dangaléat se subdivise en deux dialectes: le dangaléat de l'Est et le dangaléat de l'Ouest appelée communément Karbo. Mais il pourrait être subdivisé davantage en trois dialectes, notamment en dialecte de l'Est, du Centre et de l'Ouest. ... Le dangaléat de l'Est et du Centre épousent certaines caractéristiques tonales du bidiya qui possède trois tons ponctuels. ... il convient de souligner qu'entre le bidiya et le dangaléat, il est plutôt question de variation tonale que consonantique.
tone_statements.translation: Dangaléat divides into two dialects, East Dangaléat and West Dangaléat commonly called Karbo, but could be further divided into three: East, Centre and West. ... East and Central Dangaléat share certain tonal characteristics of Bidiya, which has three level tones. ... it should be stressed that between Bidiya and Dangaléat the variation is tonal rather than consonantal.
tone_statements.summary: East and Central Dangaléat: three level (ponctuel) tones like Bidiya (implied contrast with West); no further detail.

tone_statements.citation: Fédry, Jacques. 1969. Syntagmes de détermination en dangaléat. Journal of West African Languages 6(1): 5-19.
tone_statements.quote: Il faut nettement distinguer deux groupes dans le dialecte dangaléat: les parlers de l'ouest (Korbo, Tyalo-Idéba) et ceux de l'est, qui se différencient par un système tonal symétriquement opposé ... Les parlers dangaléat de l'ouest connaissent deux niveaux pertinents de ton, le ton haut et le ton bas ... qui, combinés, donnent deux tons modulés, descendant ... et ascendant ... Ces tons modulés ne se rencontrent pas sur voyelle brève en syllabe ouverte, mais seulement sur voyelle longue (qu'il nous paraît préférable d'interpréter comme la succession de deux phonèmes vocaliques brefs isotimbres ...).
tone_statements.translation: Two groups must be clearly distinguished within Dangaléat: the western varieties (Korbo, Tyalo-Idéba) and the eastern ones, which differ by a symmetrically opposed tone system ... The western Dangaléat varieties have two distinctive tone levels, high tone and low tone, which combined give two contour tones, falling and rising. These contour tones do not occur on a short vowel in an open syllable, only on a long vowel (which we prefer to interpret as a sequence of two identical short vowel phonemes ...).
tone_statements.locator: pp. 5-6 (introduction and 'Note sur la transcription', just before §12 'Système nominal')
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: West Dangaléat (Tyalo-Idéba): two level tones H and L; falling and rising contours only on long vowels (= sequences of two short vowels), plus falling on short V before CC from a deleted L vowel; East vs West tone systems 'symmetrically opposed'; tone also marks noun plural; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Peust, Carsten. 2017. Dangla historical tonology. Folia Orientalia 54: 201-242.
sources.tag: read: notes on stress
sources.note: p. 206: West Dangla has two contrastive tone levels (H, L), East and Central Dangla three (H, M, L) 'according to almost all investigators so far'; Arabic loans prefer HL/LH 'where high matches the Arabic stress syllable'. p. 204: Lukas 1937: 17 recorded East Dangla ('Kaṛbo') words 'with the high (and mid) tone misinterpreted as a word-accent'. p. 203: Wolff 1986: 571 posited a diachronic 'pitch accent' ('Each verb had the potential to occur both in a stressed and unstressed form'), which Peust rejects as circular. No synchronic word-stress statement for any Dangla variety.

sources.citation: Peust, Carsten. 2014. A morphological sketch of West Dangla (Chad). Folia Orientalia 51: 201-255.
sources.tag: read: notes on stress
sources.note: §2 Tone (p. 202): per Fédry's analysis each syllable bears one of four tones (high, low, falling, rising; contours only on heavy syllables) and words carry one of five word-level tone patterns (H, L, HLL, HHL, LH); §3-§6 vowel harmony, vowel quantity (contrastive only in first syllable), free vs context form. The words stress/accent/prominence do not occur in the article; phonology is explicitly deferred to Fédry 1971b. Based entirely on Fédry's West Dangla (Tyalo-Idéba) data.
